description: Conversational learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

article.title: The Friendship Paradox: Why Your Friends Have More Friends Than You Do
article.author: Dr. Jennifer Lawson

cards.title: The Friendship Paradox
cards.subtitle: Your friends have more friends than you—it's not bad luck, it's math.
body: People with many friends show up in more friend groups. The person with 100 friends gets counted in 100 averages.
It's structural, not personal. Your circle is biased toward well-connected people.
cards.takeaway: Your average friend is more connected than you; that's how the math works.

cards.title: Reciprocal Friendship Is Rare
cards.subtitle: About half the people you consider close friends may not list you back.
body: Studies find ~50% of perceived friendships aren't reciprocal.

• You list 12 close friends
• Only 6 might list you
• Friendship is often asymmetric
cards.takeaway: Reciprocity in friendship is assumed more often than verified.

cards.title: Dunbar's Number Is About Time
cards.subtitle: You could remember 500 people, but maintaining them isn't possible.
body: The ~150 limit isn't cognitive—it's time. Maintaining relationships requires regular interaction.
You're not brain-limited; you're time-limited. Quality connections need ongoing attention.
cards.takeaway: The limit on relationships is usually time, not memory.

cards.title: Proximity Creates Friendships
cards.subtitle: Your randomly-assigned roommate became one of your closest friends.
body: Repeated exposure creates familiarity and liking. Proximity often matters more than similarity.
Most friendships form from convenience. Compatibility helps once you're in the same room.
cards.takeaway: Proximity matters more than similarity in forming friendships.

cards.title: Weak Ties Provide Opportunities
cards.subtitle: Your best friend knows the same people. An acquaintance got you the job.
body: Strong ties overlap your world. Weak ties bridge to different networks.
Jobs, ideas, and opportunities often come through acquaintances, not close friends.
cards.takeaway: Weak ties provide new opportunities that strong ties don't.

cards.title: The Liking Gap
cards.subtitle: You thought the conversation was awkward; they thought you were interesting.
body: People consistently underestimate how much others enjoyed talking to them.
Others remember you more fondly than you assume. We're our own harshest critics.
cards.takeaway: You're probably a worse judge of your impression than they are.

cards.title: Relationship Satisfaction Is U-Shaped
cards.subtitle: High early, low in the middle, high again later.
body: Early years are exciting. Middle years—kids, stress, routine—satisfaction drops.
Empty-nest years often recover. The middle decline isn't failure; it's normal.
cards.takeaway: The middle years of long relationships are often hardest; that's normal.

cards.title: Geography Shapes Who You Marry
cards.subtitle: Statistically, your 'soulmate' lived within twenty miles.
body: Most people marry someone from their city, school, or workplace.
Love feels fated, but it's logistically determined. Your pool is whoever you crossed paths with.
cards.takeaway: Geography shapes who we end up with more than we acknowledge.

cards.title: Conflict Avoidance Predicts Breakups
cards.subtitle: Couples who never fight aren't in harmony—they're disengaged.
body: Avoiding conflict means issues accumulate silently. No resolution, just withdrawal.
Couples who argue constructively and repair afterward tend to last longer.
cards.takeaway: Conflict avoidance predicts breakups more than conflict itself.

cards.title: Contempt Is the Strongest Predictor of Divorce
cards.subtitle: Criticism is manageable; contempt—eye rolls, mockery—is terminal.
body: Contempt signals loss of respect. You're treating your partner as beneath you.
Criticism can be addressed. Contempt erodes the foundation and rarely heals.
cards.takeaway: Contempt is the strongest predictor of divorce; take it seriously.
